note: An echo of the Aeneid. When Queen Dido asks Aeneas to tell of the fall of Troy, he begins: "You bid me, queen, renew a grief beyond words." The speaker casts himself as the hero of a tragedy.
The traitors in the ice do not want to be remembered. This one speaks for a single reason: to blacken his enemy's name among the living. His story is an act of revenge, like his gnawing.

Almost the words of Francesca da Rimini in Inferno 5, who also tells her story through tears. Hell's two most famous speakers, near its top and at its bottom, are linked: hers is a story of love, his of hatred.
He knows Dante's city by his accent, as Farinata did in Inferno 10. Florence was Pisa's enemy, so a Florentine will be glad to carry home a story that shames Pisa.

context: He tells nothing of his own treachery, for which he is damned. He tells only how he died, and what was done to his children.
He never speaks. A traitor to his ally, he is frozen just below his victim, who feeds on him forever: the man he starved now has him as food.

quote: I trusted him and was made prisoner
note: In 1288 Ruggieri made common cause with Ugolino against Ugolino's own grandson and rival, Nino Visconti. Once Nino was driven out, the archbishop raised the people of Pisa against Ugolino and seized him. All Tuscany knew the story, so Ugolino passes over it.

A tower in Pisa belonging to the Gualandi family, called the Muda, the Mew, perhaps because the city's eagles were kept there while they moulted. After Ugolino and his children starved in it, it was known as the Tower of Hunger. It was still used as a prison in Dante's day.
Several months. Ugolino was locked up in the summer of 1288 and died early in 1289.
In the dream, Ugolino and his children are a wolf and its cubs, and the archbishop is master of the hunt. The dream tells him how it will end before the tower door is shut.

Monte Pisano, also called Monte San Giuliano, the ridge between Pisa and Lucca. Lucca was a Guelph city where Ugolino might have hoped for shelter, so the wolf is being run down on the road to safety.
Three leading Ghibelline families of Pisa, who joined the archbishop against Ugolino. In the dream they ride at the front of the hunt, and the lean hounds are the mob of the city.

In fact two sons, Gaddo and Uguccione, and two grandsons, Nino, called Brigata, and Anselmuccio. All but Anselmuccio were grown men. Dante makes the four of them young, helpless children, which makes their deaths harder to bear.

The Italian word can also mean simply that the door was locked, but nailed shut is the likelier sense. The chroniclers say the keys were thrown into the Arno. Until then the prisoners had been fed. The sound tells Ugolino that no more food will come.

quote: I had turned to stone within
note: Through the whole ordeal Ugolino says nothing to his children: no comfort, no prayer. Many readers see in this silence the hardness of heart that damned him, even as they pity him.
Anselmuccio, the younger of the two grandsons, probably about fifteen.

The children speak in the language of the Bible, echoing Job: "You clothed me with skin and flesh", and "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away." Their offer to be eaten is one of selfless love, and it prepares the terrible doubt of Ugolino's last line.
One of Ugolino's sons. His dying words recall Christ's cry on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). Ugolino, the father who cannot help, has no answer.
This puts Ugolino's own death on the eighth day. Older editions of the poem read three days here, and many older translations follow them.

quote: hunger accomplished what grief could not
note: One of the most argued lines in the poem. In the Italian: "Then fasting had more power than grief." The usual reading is that hunger killed him when grief had not. But the words can also mean that hunger overcame his grief and he ate his children's bodies. Dante leaves it unsaid, and Ugolino's eternal gnawing keeps the darker reading alive.

context: Dante breaks off the story to curse the whole city. His anger is not for Ugolino's death but for the killing of the children with him.

note: Italy. Dante sorted the languages descended from Latin by their word for yes: oc in the south of France, oïl in the north, and sì in Italy.
Florence and Lucca, the Guelph cities that were Pisa's old enemies.

Two small islands in the sea off the Tuscan coast, which then belonged to Pisa. The Arno flows through Pisa a few miles before it reaches the sea. Dante imagines the islands sliding across to block the river mouth, so that the water backs up and drowns the city.

In 1285, after Genoa had crushed the Pisan fleet, Ugolino handed several Pisan castles to Florence and Lucca. It may have been a sound move to split the alliance against Pisa, but his enemies called it treason. This is probably the betrayal that puts him in Antenora. Dante's wording leaves open whether the charge was true.
The word joins the children to Christ, innocent victims put to death for another's guilt.
The other two: Uguccione, Ugolino's son, and Nino, called Brigata, his grandson. With Anselmuccio and Gaddo, named in the story, they make up the four.

context: Pisa has made itself a new Thebes, the city where kinsmen destroyed each other and the innocent died with the guilty.

note: The third zone of the ice, named a little further on. The souls here lie on their backs with their faces turned up. Their heads can no longer bend, so their tears pool in the eye sockets and freeze into a mask of ice. Even the relief of weeping is taken from them.

Medieval science held that wind is caused by the sun's heat drawing vapors up from the earth. No sun reaches here, so there should be no wind. The cause is revealed in Canto 34: the beating of Lucifer's wings.
The soul takes Dante and Virgil for damned traitors on their way to the last and lowest zone of the ice.

quote: may I go to the bottom of the ice
note: A trick oath. Dante is going to the bottom of the ice in any case, as a visitor. The soul takes it as a solemn promise.

Alberigo dei Manfredi of Faenza, a member of the Jovial Friars, the lay order whose hypocrites Dante met in Inferno 23. In 1285, after a family quarrel, he invited two kinsmen, Manfred and his son Alberghetto, to dinner as a sign of peace, and had them murdered at the table.

quote: the fruit from the evil garden
note: At the end of the meal Alberigo called out, "Bring the fruit." It was the signal for his men to come in and kill the guests. "Friar Alberigo's fruit" became a saying.

quote: a date in return for my fig
note: Dates were dearer than figs. He is being paid back with interest, he says, with the bitter humor of the fruit still on his mind.
Dante is astonished because in the spring of 1300, when the journey takes place, Alberigo was known to be alive. He lived for some years more.

context: Its "advantage", spoken with bitter irony, is that it does not wait for death. The soul of one who betrays a guest drops here at once.

note: One of the three Fates of Greek myth. Clotho spins the thread of each life, Lachesis measures it, and Atropos cuts it.

Dante's own invention, and a daring one, since the Church teaches that anyone may repent until the moment of death. It may draw on the Gospel of John, where Satan enters into Judas at the Last Supper. It also lets Dante put living men in Hell.

A nobleman of the great Doria family of Genoa. He invited his father-in-law, Michele Zanche, to a banquet and had him cut down, to get hold of his lands in Sardinia. He was alive in 1300 and for many years afterward.

context: Alberigo points back up to the ditch of the boiling pitch, where Branca's victim is punished.
Branca's soul fell to the ice so fast that it arrived before his murdered victim had reached his own place in Hell.

note: A relative of Branca's, said to be a nephew or cousin, who helped in the murder. His name is not known.

quote: To be rude to him was courtesy
note: Dante breaks his word to a traitor and calls it good manners. Virgil taught him in Inferno 20 that pity for the damned questions God's judgment. Some readers still find it troubling that he answers treachery with a small treachery of his own.
The people of Genoa, the great port and sea power of northwest Italy. This is the second curse on a whole city in one canto, after Pisa. The two were bitter rivals.
Friar Alberigo. His city, Faenza, is in Romagna, the region east of the Apennines between Bologna and the Adriatic.
